From Cardinal Passionei’s opinion of 1753, written for Benedict XIV on the question of the canonization of Cardinal Robert Bellarmine.
The issue concerns Bellarmine’s autobiography “from faith,” which he wrote in 1613, at the age of seventy-one, at the request of a friend.
May a person write his own life?
May he keep a diary intended to be read by other people?

Answer: a Christian may not do so because of the duty of humilitas—humility. He may do it only on the order of a Church superior or confessor, through divine inspiration, or because he is forced to defend himself.
In his Confessions, Augustine spoke only of things that counted against him.

Faced with this objection, some defenders of Bellarmine tried to dismiss his autobiography as something insignificant: a relatiuncula, a scriptiuncula, a breviculum, a notila— a tiny report, a little piece of writing, a brief note.
Others say: writing one’s own life is morally neutral in itself. One might even do it out of humility.

Passionei answers: it is at the very least an occasio proxima, a near occasion, of the most dangerous sin of all: self-love and pride. And because these are sins of the spirit, they are more dangerous than lust.
“Our deeds are our beloved daughters, our all-too-beautiful wives, to whom we are drawn again and again, whose beauty we gaze upon with self-satisfaction, like Lucifer and our father Adam.”

Occupying oneself with one’s own autobiography is therefore just as much an occasion for sin as, for a young man, spending time with a young, beautiful, all-too-lovable woman whom he passionately wishes to be alone with and with whom he wants to speak freely and intimately.
